Definition
In this lesson you are taught the concept of amplitude modulation and will observe amplitude modulated signals.
INTRODUCTIONM
Amplitude Modulation, AM, is the simplest form of signal processing, it has been used since the first days of radio.
AM systems have several limitations that other methods of modulation overcome.
AM is used in many types of communication systems because of simple circuits, proven reliability, and low cost.
Let's begin the lesson on AMPLITUDE MODULATION............................
LESSON MENU
AMPLITUDE MODULATION
Amplitude Modulation, AM, is used to convey information from a source to a destination through a transmission medium.
DISCUSSION
Amplitude modulation is a signal processing technique that modifies a carrier signal by the information signal.
The modification allows the information signal to be sent over long distances, where the information signal itself could not be sent.
The name amplitude modulation is derived from how the carrier signal is modified, in amplitude.
In transmitter signal processing, a constant amplitude carrier signal is developed by an oscillator.
The carrier signal is then fed to an AM modulator circuit.
The second input to the modulator circuit is the information signal.
The modulator circuit causes the amplitude of the carrier signal to change according to the amplitude of the information signal.
Notice the positive and negative alternation of the AM signal. The information signal modulates a positive wave and negative wave.
The resultant AM signal is then transmitted through the transmission medium (most commonly air but, could be; cables, microwaves or fiber optic cables).
In the receiver signal processing, the transmitted AM signal is picked up through a tuning process and the information signal is recovered.
There are many AM signals available. The tuning circuits allow you to select which AM signal to process.
The detector circuits separate the carrier signal from the information signal.
The information signal is then sent to amplifiers for further processing.

CARRIER FREQUENCY
For modulation, the carrier signal must be at a higher frequency than the information signal.
For example, to transmit and receive your voice (approximately 40 Hz to 4 kHz), the carrier signal must be greater than 4 kHz.
To transmit the full range of your hearing, a higher carrier signal is needed because of the higher information frequencies (from around 40 Hz to 20 kHz).
As a rule of thumb, the carrier frequency must be at least 50 times greater than the highest information frequency for proper operation of communication electronic circuits.
Look at an AM radio, the carrier frequencies range from 540 kHz to 1600 kHz.
Even at a lower frequency of 540 kHz, the carrier frequency is over 50 times higher than your highest voice frequency (approximately 5 kHz).

BANDWIDTH
Bandwidth is a limiting factor in a communication system.
Since the carrier frequency limits the maximum information signal frequency, the carrier frequency also limits bandwidth.

For example, the lowest AM radio frequency is 540 kHz allowing a bandwidth of 10.8 kHz.
The bandwidth (10.8 kHz) for a carrier frequency of 540 kHz is fine for voice transmissions such as news and weather stations.
But, for high quality music transmissions (frequencies up to approximately 20 kHz), the bandwidth is insufficient and fidelity is lost.
DEFINITION

FIDELITY - The extent to which a signal is transmitted and received without distortion. Distortion is a change in the wave form of a signal caused by nonuniform transmission and reception at different frequencies.
But, for high quality music transmissions (frequencies up to approximately 20 kHz), the bandwidth is insufficient and fidelity is lost.
An important point about bandwidth is that the higher the carrier frequency, the wider the bandwidth or, the more information that can be processed.

SIDEBAND
Sideband is the frequency above and below a center frequency. In our case a sideband is a frequency above or below a carrier frequency.
The sidebands around a carrier frequency are produced by the modulating signal or information signal. Let's see why.
Up to this point you may be thinking that an AM signal is composed of two completely different signals - the carrier and modulating signal.
Actually, the AM signal is one signal produced by the carrier and modulating signal. It is a complex waveform.
If you used a spectrum analyzer to find the frequencies that make up the AM signal, you would find the carrier signal and the sidebands, not the carrier signal and modulating signals!

For example, if a 600 kHz carrier signal is amplitude modulated with a 10 kHz information signal, the frequencies that make up the AM waveform are 590 kHz, 600 kHz and 610 kHz. They are not 600 kHz and 10 kHz.
c, at 600 kHz and the sideband frequencies of 590 and 610 kHz.
The 590 kHz sideband is called the Lower Sideband because it is below the carrier frequency.
The 610 kHz sideband is called the Upper Sideband because it is above the carrier frequency.
The sideband frequencies are calculated by:................
max = Highest Modulation Frequency or Bandwidth
Sideband frequencies are very important in AM communication systems, they determine the spacing between different AM stations or channels.
The AM radio band uses 10 kHz spacing between stations. If the full bandwidth of a 600 kHz carrier signal is used, the sidebands would interfere with stations at 590 and 610 kHz.
This is why AM stations are limited to bandwidths of 5 kHz. This produces sidebands of 595 and 605 kHz for a 600 kHz carrier frequency - no interference of adjacent channels.

PERCENT MODULATION
Percent modulation is the amount the carrier signal is modulated and is expressed as a percent.
Percent Modulation is an expression of the amount of power in the information signal.
Modulation levels normally range from 0% to 100%. Where 0% is no modulation and 100% is full modulation.
The higher the percent modulation or level, the more power in the information signal.

Noise is a limiting factor in a communications system.
Noise is variations in voltage or current no matter if produced by atmospheric conditions or by thermal noise.
Noise is variations in voltage or current no matter if produced by atmospheric conditions or by thermal noise.
DEFINITION

THERMAL NOISE - Thermal noise is caused by temperature variations in electronic components. At any temperature above absolute zero, electrons exhibit random motion. The random motion results in the generation of voltages or currents which cause noise.
These variations in voltage and current are amplitude variations. Of course any amplitude variation in an AM signal is processed as information.
Consequently, noise in an AM signal can not be eliminated. Circuits may be designed to reduce noise but, can not eliminate noise altogether.
You probably have noticed that AM stations are noisier than FM stations. If you get a chance, compare an AM station to an FM station.
DEFINITION
FM - FM stands for frequency modulation. The information signal is contained in frequency variations. Since noise affects signal amplitude, it has practically no effect on FM signals.
The sideband frequencies also produce a bandwidth for the AM signal.
As shown, a 10 kHz modulating signal produces sideband frequencies of 590 and 610 kHz, a bandwidth of 20 kHz.
This sideband bandwidth (20kHz) is twice the bandwidth of the modulating signal (10kHz).
The bandwidth of the AM signal must be considered when designing AM communication systems.
